content:
Erik Ninn-Hansen (1922–2014) was a Danish conservative politician and lawyer best known—beyond a long parliamentary and ministerial career—for his central role in the “Tamil case,” the most consequential Danish political-legal scandal of the late 20th century.

Key facts
- Full name: Erik Ib Schmidt Ninn-Hansen
- Born: 13 April 1922, on Bornholm (Aakirkeby)
- Died: 20 September 2014
- Party: The Conservative People’s Party (Det Konservative Folkeparti)
- Profession: Lawyer (cand.jur.); practiced as an attorney before and between political posts
- Member of the Folketing: 1953–1994 (Bornholm constituency)
- Party leadership: Conservative party leader (chairman), 1971–1974

Government and parliamentary offices
- Minister of Justice:
  - 1968–1971 (Hilmar Baunsgaard’s government)
  - 1982–1987 (Poul Schlüter’s first governments)
  - He also held top posts immediately after 1987; he served as Speaker of the Folketing 1987–1989. Some sources note a brief later stint as Justice Minister around 1989–1990 before resigning as the Tamil case gathered force.
- Speaker of the Folketing (Folketingets formand): 1987–1989

The Tamil case (Tamilsagen)
- Core issue: In 1987, while Justice Minister, Ninn-Hansen gave instructions to the immigration authorities to halt or markedly delay family reunification applications by Tamil refugees from Sri Lanka who held temporary residence in Denmark. These directions ran counter to the Aliens Act and to Parliament’s intent.
- Discovery and inquiry: As the pattern of refusals/delays emerged, political pressure led to investigations, culminating in the Tamil Commission (Tamilkommissionen). Its findings (released in early 1993) concluded the instructions were unlawful and that Parliament had been misled.
- Political fallout: The report triggered the fall of Prime Minister Poul Schlüter’s government in January 1993.
- Legal outcome: Ninn-Hansen was impeached before the Danish Court of Impeachment (Rigsretten)—the first such case in many decades. In 1995 he was convicted for abuse of office related to the illegal instructions; he received a 4‑month suspended prison sentence.
- Party consequences: He left/was expelled from the Conservative parliamentary group during the scandal period and finished his career outside the party’s fold. He left the Folketing in the mid‑1990s (1994).

Reputation and legacy
- Supporters long viewed him as a forceful, disciplined conservative figure—tough on law-and-order and immigration, influential in shaping the Conservative Party in the post‑war period.
- Historically, however, his name is inseparable from the Tamil case, which became a touchstone for rule-of-law norms in Danish governance: it tested ministerial responsibility, civil‑service independence, and truthful ministerial accountability to Parliament. The Rigsret conviction stands as a rare and landmark assertion of legal limits on executive discretion in Denmark.

Notes on uncertainties
- Open-source accounts differ slightly on whether he briefly returned as Justice Minister in 1989–1990 after serving as Speaker; the Tamil case itself stems from his 1987 instructions during his 1982–1987 Justice Ministry. The conviction and the political consequences outlined above are consistent across authoritative sources.
